cells.tense: What's coming in right now is being met on purpose, a piece at a time rather than all at once.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to yourself, the one ending you've already settled and haven't announced
cells.core:
When something you're part of reaches its edge, you close it without a speech and stay friendly at the same table the next week. You can tell finished from hard, and you don't need a ceremony to put down what's used up. So when something new shows up, you make room for it first and sort the rest later.

What arrives next usually comes right after something leaves, and you've stopped pretending otherwise. Name the ending you've already decided and haven't said yet — that's the whole ask. Half the weight goes the moment it's spoken, because you stop carrying two versions of the same week, and the thing that's arriving gets to land in one true place instead of two.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's finished from what's merely difficult.
cells.verb: letting what has finished finish, so what's next can start
cells.place: what's arriving now, at the moment it comes in

cells.tense: You're past the next ending before it happens, already braced for the one after that.
cells.ask: Text one person the plain state of something unfinished you're in — no closing, just where it actually stands today
cells.core:
When this part is working, you let things run to their real edge and handle them there — a job kept until it was actually done, a friendship left to take its own shape. You can wait for a thing to finish on its own schedule, and you usually do.

The endings are coming faster than anything has had time to live. From inside, it feels like getting ahead of something, and the word for it might be clearing out. But it could be keeping you from standing still long enough to be caught by an ending you didn't pick. Send one person the plain state of something unfinished. No close. The bracing eases when one thing gets to stay exactly as it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've had a chance to happen.
cells.verb: letting what has finished finish, so what's next can start
cells.place: what's arriving now, at the moment it comes in

cells.tense: You're still at a door you closed, standing with the key in your hand.
cells.ask: Pick one object that belongs to something over, put it out of your daily reach, and leave it there
cells.core:
On a good day you pick up what's arriving because something kept going after the old thing stopped. You start the new way, you make the call, you clear a shelf for the thing that's coming and let the other one stay where it was.

What's hard here is that staying gets called loyalty, and it may be holding you past what's real. Choose one thing — a mug, a ticket stub, a shirt — and move it out of daily reach today, without throwing it away. That small move doesn't decide anything. It just lets you find out whether anything moves after it, and whether the next thing coming has somewhere to land.

cells.tense: You're standing in a version of your life that's already ended, and the page underneath is blank.
cells.ask: Clear one surface today — a desk, a table, one shelf — and leave it empty rather than refilling it with the same things
cells.core:
When you're aware of it, you clear room before the next thing comes — you tidy the desk before you sit down to start. An ordinary move that lets what's coming land somewhere with space for it, and you do it without making a thing of it.

Your hands have already been clearing something; you haven't said which, or maybe that anything is. It might be why things feel slightly off — the floor has shifted and you're still walking the old route. Clear one surface today and leave it empty. Not as a statement. You don't have to know what it's for. It just gives the next thing something true to arrive into.
